claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farley, 1969.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis.
claims.source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969 (Farley, 1969), and has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis (Green and Alderman, 1983; Lowe and Moore, 1978; Rasmussen, 1986) and M. galloprovincialis (Ciocan and Sunila, 2005; Carella et al., 2013; Gombač et al., 2013), albeit at lower prevalence than has been observed in some M. trossulus populations, which reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses (Barber, 2004; Bower et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in M. trossulus reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses.
claims.source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in marine mussels as early as 1969 (Farley, 1969), and has been observed consistently throughout Europe in both M. edulis (Green and Alderman, 1983; Lowe and Moore, 1978; Rasmussen, 1986) and M. galloprovincialis (Ciocan and Sunila, 2005; Carella et al., 2013; Gombač et al., 2013), albeit at lower prevalence than has been observed in some M. trossulus populations, which reached >20% in some locations in the 1980s and was associated with population losses (Barber, 2004; Bower et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Barber, 2004 and Bower et al., 1994.

claims.claim: Mussels in the genus Mytilus form a complex of species including M. trossulus, M. edulis, M. galloprovincialis (native to the northern hemisphere) and M. chilensis, M. platensis, and M. planulatus (native to the southern hemisphere).
claims.source: Mussels in the genus Mytilus form a complex of species, including M. trossulus, M. edulis, and M. galloprovincialis, native to the northern hemisphere, and M. chilensis, M. platensis, and M. planulatus, native to the southern hemisphere (Zbawicka et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zbawicka et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Mytilus species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world.
claims.source: These species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world, and they can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles (Fraïsse et al., 2016) as well as hybrid zones in several locations (Bierne et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on Mytilus distribution.

claims.claim: Mytilus species can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles and hybrid zones in several locations.
claims.source: These species have an anti-tropical distribution, spanning the temperate waters of the world, and they can hybridize, leading to widespread introgression of allospecific alleles (Fraïsse et al., 2016) as well as hybrid zones in several locations (Bierne et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fraïsse et al., 2016 and Bierne et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four Mytilus species across multiple continents.
claims.source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four of these Mytilus species across multiple continents (Barber, 2004; Carballal et al., 2015), but so far the only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia (BC), Canada (Metzger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus Mytilus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer prior to this study is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia, Canada.
claims.source: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in four of these Mytilus species across multiple continents (Barber, 2004; Carballal et al., 2015), but so far the only lineage of disseminated neoplasia in the genus that has been directly confirmed to be a transmissible cancer is in M. trossulus along the Pacific coast of British Columbia (BC), Canada (Metzger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metzger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: A population genetics analysis of M. edulis from France identified individuals with unexpected 'chimeric' signals containing M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent.
claims.source: A population genetics analysis of M. edulis from France, conducted to detect hybridization and introgression between Mytilus species by detecting species-specific SNPs, identified a few individuals with unexpected 'chimeric' signals. The DNA samples from these individuals included M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent, and the ratio of the M. edulis and M. trossulus alleles were not consistent with a diploid hybrid genome. Instead, this could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual (Riquet et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riquet et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The 'chimeric' signals in M. edulis from France could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual rather than a diploid hybrid genome.
claims.source: The DNA samples from these individuals included M. trossulus alleles in a population where that species was absent, and the ratio of the M. edulis and M. trossulus alleles were not consistent with a diploid hybrid genome. Instead, this could be better explained by a mixture of two genotypes (one M. edulis and one M. trossulus in origin) within a single individual (Riquet et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riquet et al., 2017 and represents an inference from genetic data.

claims.claim: A severe mass mortality event in French mussels began in 2014.
claims.source: More recently, analysis of a severe mass mortality event (Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016) in French mussels that began in 2014 led to the observation of disseminated neoplasia in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis (Benadelmouna et al., 2018), although it has not yet been determined whether this neoplasia is transmissible.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia was observed in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis following a mass mortality event in French mussels.
claims.source: More recently, analysis of a severe mass mortality event (Benabdelmouna and Ledu, 2016) in French mussels that began in 2014 led to the observation of disseminated neoplasia in many populations of M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis (Benadelmouna et al., 2018), although it has not yet been determined whether this neoplasia is transmissible.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benadelmouna et al., 2018.

claims.claim: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America.
claims.source: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America, and disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations in Chile and Argentina since 1998 (Lohrmann et al., 2019; Cremonte et al., 2015; Campalans et al., 1998; Cremonte et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of M. chilensis distribution.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations of M. chilensis in Chile and Argentina since 1998.
claims.source: M. chilensis mussels are found along the western coast of South America, and disseminated neoplasia has been reported in multiple populations in Chile and Argentina since 1998 (Lohrmann et al., 2019; Cremonte et al., 2015; Campalans et al., 1998; Cremonte et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in M. chilensis has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina.
claims.source: Prevalence has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina, although no notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in these populations.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from the study or prior observations.

claims.claim: No notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in M. chilensis populations.
claims.source: Prevalence has varied by location, ranging from undetectable in some populations to as high as 12% in the Castro region of Chile and 13% in the Beagle Channel in southern Argentina, although no notable mass mortality events have been associated with neoplasia in these populations.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from the study or prior research.

claims.claim: Mytilus BTN1 was able to be distinguished from normal M. trossulus genotypes at both a nuclear and mitochondrial locus.
claims.source: Mytilus BTN1 was able to be distinguished from normal M. trossulus genotypes at both a nuclear and mitochondrial locus (Metzger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metzger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: 60 M. chilensis animals were collected from Argentina in 2012 with a disease prevalence of 10%.
claims.source: To determine whether the disseminated neoplasia in M. chilensis was due to a conventional cancer or a transmissible cancer lineage, we collected 60 M. chilensis animals from Argentina in 2012. Histological analysis was used to diagnose the animals for the presence of disseminated neoplasia, and we observed a disease prevalence of 10%.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from the study.

claims.claim: Two of three diseased M. chilensis animals (Mch41 and Mch42) had four distinct EF1α alleles, consistent with a mixture of two host alleles and two cancer-specific alleles.
claims.source: All three normal animals had one or two alleles, as expected, but two of the diseased animals (Mch41 and Mch42) had four distinct alleles, consistent with a mixture of two host alleles and two cancer-specific alleles (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Two alleles (G and H) from diseased M. chilensis animal Mch41 were nearly exact matches to two alleles from Mch42, consistent with the presence of a transmissible cancer.
claims.source: Notably, each diseased sample had two alleles that were unique (corresponding to host alleles), but two alleles from animal Mch41 were nearly exact matches to two alleles from Mch42 (here notated as G and H). This is consistent with the presence of a transmissible cancer containing alleles G and H.
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and represents an inference about transmissible cancer.

claims.claim: EF1α alleles cloned from a diseased M. chilensis individual from Chile exactly match the G and H cancer-associated sequences from Argentina.
claims.source: A second collection of farmed M. chilensis from two locations in Chile confirmed the presence of disseminated neoplasia in these populations (9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro). EF1α alleles cloned from a diseased individual from this location exactly match the G and H cancer-associated sequences from Argentina.
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: Disseminated neoplasia prevalence in farmed M. chilensis from Chile was 9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro.
claims.source: A second collection of farmed M. chilensis from two locations in Chile confirmed the presence of disseminated neoplasia in these populations (9.6% in Calbuco and 4.5% in Castro).
claims.evidence: This is based on data from the study.

claims.claim: Phylogenetic analysis shows that the cancer-associated EF1α alleles (G and H) are likely of M. trossulus or M. chilensis origin.
claims.source: Phylogenetic analysis of these putative cancer-associated alleles shows that they are likely of M. trossulus or M. chilensis origin (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Both cancer-associated EF1α alleles (G and H) are clearly distinct from normal M. trossulus individuals and distinct from either allele of Mytilus BTN1.
claims.source: However, both cancer-associated alleles are clearly distinct from normal M. trossulus individuals and distinct from either allele of the previously identified BC transmissible neoplasia, Mytilus BTN1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The EF1α S allele from Mytilus BTN1 is closely related to a subset of normal M. trossulus alleles.
claims.source: Additionally, phylogenetic analysis shows that the EF1α S allele from Mytilus BTN1 (previously termed the 'minor' allele) is closely related to a subset of normal M. trossulus alleles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic tree is incompatible with the cancer-associated G and H alleles arising from the same cancer lineage as the Mytilus BTN1 S allele.
claims.source: Thus, the tree is incompatible with the cancer-associated G and H alleles arising from the same cancer lineage as the Mytilus BTN1 S allele, although analysis of additional loci is needed to confirm this finding.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The BTN found in M. chilensis likely represents a separate, independent lineage of transmissible cancer, called Mytilus BTN2.
claims.source: The BTN found in M. chilensis therefore likely represents a separate, independent lineage of transmissible cancer, here called Mytilus BTN2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic and genetic data.

claims.claim: More than the normal two EF1α alleles were found in three of four 'chimeric' M. edulis samples from the Atlantic coast of Europe.
claims.source: We sequenced the EF1α alleles present in DNA from four of these 'chimeric' samples of M. edulis collected from locations on the Atlantic coast of Europe and found more than the normal two alleles in three of them (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Only one or two EF1α alleles were observed in normal M. edulis from the same populations.
claims.source: Only one or two alleles were observed in normal M. edulis from the same populations.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: Two cancer-associated EF1α alleles found in diseased M. edulis exactly matched those found in cancer samples from M. chilensis in South America (Mytilus BTN2).
claims.source: Unexpectedly, these two cancer-associated alleles found in diseased M. edulis did not match the previously reported Mytilus BTN1 lineage, found in M. trossulus in Canada, but instead exactly matched those found in cancer samples from M. chilensis in South America (Mytilus BTN2) (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In European M. edulis cancer samples, alleles identical to the G allele from M. chilensis and two nearly identical versions of the H allele (H and H') were found.
claims.source: In these European M. edulis cancer samples, we found alleles identical to the G allele from M. chilensis and two nearly identical versions of the H allele, with only one SNP between them (termed H').
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: The H' allele likely represents a true second copy of the H allele within the cancer cells, consistent with a de novo mutation which occurred in one copy of the H allele after genome duplication.
claims.source: Both the H and H' alleles were represented by multiple clones and found in multiple individuals, so H' likely represents a true second copy of the H allele within the cancer cells. Disseminated neoplasia is polyploid, and this result is consistent with a de novo mutation which occurred in one copy of the H allele after genome duplication (and likely after divergence of the South American and European strains of this lineage).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data and knowledge of polyploidy in disseminated neoplasia.

claims.claim: 2-5 H4 alleles were observed in diseased M. chilensis and M. edulis samples and only 1-2 in normal samples.
claims.source: We observed 2–5 alleles in diseased samples and only 1–2 in normal samples (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Looking only at normal H4 alleles, there is a clear grouping based on species of origin in a phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: Looking only at normal alleles, there is a clear grouping based on species of origin in a phylogenetic tree (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Two sets of cancer-associated H4 alleles were identified from both M. chilensis and M. edulis, which group together.
claims.source: Two sets of cancer-associated alleles were identified from both M. chilensis and M. edulis, which group together.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: The H4 alleles associated with cancer in M. chilensis and M. edulis are distinct from the sequences of Mytilus BTN1 found in M. trossulus from Canada.
claims.source: As with EF1α, the alleles associated with cancer in M. chilensis and M. edulis are distinct from the sequences of Mytilus BTN1 found in M. trossulus from Canada.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: There are H4 alleles found in normal M. trossulus individuals that are exact matches to alleles found in both Mytilus BTN1 and Mytilus BTN2.
claims.source: Notably, there are alleles found in normal M. trossulus individuals that are exact matches to alleles found in both Mytilus BTN1 and Mytilus BTN2.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: Mytilus BTN1 likely arose within an M. trossulus individual with a 2A H4 allele and Mytilus BTN2 arose from a different M. trossulus individual which carried both MR-like and KNS-like alleles.
claims.source: Mytilus BTN1 likely arose within an M. trossulus individual with a 2A H4 allele and Mytilus BTN2 arose from a different M. trossulus individual which carried both MR-like and KNS-like alleles.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic and sequencing data.

claims.claim: Mytilus mussels have double uniparental inheritance of mitochondria, in which all individuals inherit mitochondria maternally, but a second male-specific lineage of mitochondria is also passed down to male offspring gonads.
claims.source: As Mytilus mussels have double uniparental inheritance of mitochondria (in which all individuals inherit mitochondria maternally, but a second male-specific lineage of mitochondria is also passed down to male offspring gonads), we amplified a female allele from all individuals, and both female and male alleles from about half of the individuals (10 of 21 total) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Mytilus mitochondrial inheritance.

claims.claim: A M. trossulus-like mitochondrial control region allele (termed 'D') was amplified from cancer samples from both M. edulis and M. chilensis.
claims.source: In addition, we amplified a M. trossulus-like allele from cancer samples from both M. edulis and M. chilensis. This allele (termed 'D') is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The D mitochondrial control region allele is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end.
claims.source: This allele (termed 'D') is mostly female-like, but it switches to male-like sequence at the 3' end (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The D mitochondrial control region recombinant sequence closely matches a recombinant sequence previously reported in a Baltic M. trossulus individual.
claims.source: This recombinant sequence closely matches a recombinant sequence previously reported in a Baltic M. trossulus individual (Śmietanka and Burzyński, 2017; Zbawicka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: A second M. trossulus-like mitochondrial control region allele (C) was found in all three cancer samples of M. chilensis, which represents a recombination between female and male sequences with a different recombination point than the D allele.
claims.source: Interestingly, a second M. trossulus-like allele (C) was found in all three cancer samples of M. chilensis, which also represents a recombination between female and male sequences, but with a different recombination point than the first.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: The presence of two recombinant mitochondrial control region alleles (C and D) argues for heteroplasmy of the cancer cells in M. chilensis.
claims.source: This argues for heteroplasmy of the cancer cells in M. chilensis, and either loss of this heteroplasmy in the cancer lineage infecting M. edulis or capture of this new mitochondrial genome in the cancer lineage infecting M. chilensis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claims.claim: The unique recombinant mitochondrial control region alleles argue that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 represent distinct lineages of cancer.
claims.source: These unique recombinants between female and male sequences again argue that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 represent distinct lineages of cancer.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claims.claim: Both mitochondrial control region alleles (C and D) are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage.
claims.source: Even when considering only the region without any recombination with the male sequence (Figure 3C), both of these mitochondrial alleles are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage, and the phylogenetic tree suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic tree of mitochondrial control region alleles suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
claims.source: Even when considering only the region without any recombination with the male sequence (Figure 3C), both of these mitochondrial alleles are distinct from those found in normal animals and from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage, and the phylogenetic tree suggests that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Standard 'universal' molluscan primers used for barcoding did not amplify the mtCOI allele from Mytilus BTN2.
claims.source: Standard 'universal' molluscan primers used for barcoding (Folmer et al., 1994) did not amplify the mtCOI allele from Mytilus BTN2, but by using degenerate primers flanking the region, we were able to amplify and sequence mtCOI from all samples (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data from the study.

claims.claim: A clear separation of the mtCOI mitogenomes of all three Mytilus species was identified, with the mtCOI from both Mytilus BTN1 and 2 nested within the M. trossulus sequences.
claims.source: We identified a clear separation of the mitogenomes of all three species, with the mtCOI from both Mytilus BTN1 and 2 nested within the M. trossulus sequences, as with the three other loci tested (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The Mytilus BTN1 mtCOI allele (U) showed clear differences from the Mytilus BTN2 allele (B).
claims.source: The Mytilus BTN1 allele (U) again showed clear differences from the Mytilus BTN2 allele (B).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: The closest published mtCOI sequence to the Mytilus BTN2 allele is the sequence from 62mc10, a normal M. trossulus from the Baltic region.
claims.source: As in the mitochondrial control region, the closest published sequence to the Mytilus BTN2 allele is the sequence from 62mc10, a normal M. trossulus from the Baltic region.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with published sequences.

claims.claim: The mtCOI data provide evidence that the two lineages of transmissible cancer (Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2) arose from distinct M. trossulus individuals.
claims.source: This again provides evidence that the two lineages of transmissible cancer arose from distinct M. trossulus individuals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from sequencing and phylogenetic data.

claims.claim: While the B mtCOI allele was found in Mytilus BTN2 samples from both Europe and Argentina, it was not identified in the M. chilensis samples from Chile.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, while the B allele was found in Mytilus BTN2 samples from both Europe and Argentina, it was not identified in the M. chilensis samples from Chile.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: The Chilean M. chilensis samples show evidence of the common Mytilus BTN2 alleles at all other nuclear and mitochondrial loci, suggesting recombination between cancer and host mitochondria.
claims.source: These samples show evidence of the common Mytilus BTN2 alleles at all other nuclear and mitochondrial loci, so this suggests that there has been recombination between cancer and host mitochondria somewhere in the M. chilensis population, resulting in a subset of Mytilus BTN2 cells in Chile with new recombinant mitogenomes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from sequencing data.

claims.claim: qPCR showed that the cancer-associated EF1α allele was found in all three M. chilensis samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23.
claims.source: Analysis of the M. chilensis samples showed that the cancer-associated allele was found in all three samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23 (Figure 5), and it was undetectable in all three normal samples.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The cancer-associated EF1α allele was undetectable in all three normal M. chilensis samples from Argentina by qPCR.
claims.source: Analysis of the M. chilensis samples showed that the cancer-associated allele was found in all three samples from Argentina that were diagnosed as diseased, including Mch23 (Figure 5), and it was undetectable in all three normal samples.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated EF1α allele, but the other two did not.
claims.source: In the M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, however, we found that two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated allele, but the other two did not. They likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claims.claim: Two diseased M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
claims.source: In the M. chilensis from the Pacific Ocean, however, we found that two of the four diseased animals had high levels of the cancer-associated allele, but the other two did not. They likely have either conventional cancer or a different transmissible cancer lineage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from qPCR data.

claims.claim: qPCR showed the presence of the cancer-associated EF1α allele in all M. edulis mussels diagnosed as diseased but not in normal samples.
claims.source: In M. edulis, qPCR showed the presence of the cancer-associated allele in all mussels diagnosed as diseased but not in normal samples.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claims.claim: The allele associated with Mytilus BTN2 in M. edulis and M. chilensis was undetectable in both normal and diseased M. trossulus samples from Canada by qPCR.
claims.source: To test whether Mytilus BTN2 could be present in the Canadian individuals at a low level, qPCR analysis was conducted on the original samples from which Mytilus BTN1 was identified (Metzger et al., 2016). The allele associated with Mytilus BTN2 in M. edulis and M. chilensis was undetectable in both normal and diseased M. trossulus samples from Canada.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claims.claim: Both cancer-associated H4 alleles were detected by qPCR in all animals diagnosed as diseased except for the two Chilean samples that were negative for the cancer-associated EF1α allele.
claims.source: qPCR primers specific for both cancer-associated H4 alleles were made, and both were detected in all animals diagnosed as diseased except for the two Chilean samples that were negative for the cancer-associated EF1α allele (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: One H4 cancer-associated allele was present at a higher level within each diseased animal than the other, but the ratio of the two alleles was not completely consistent across all individuals.
claims.source: One allele was present at a higher level within each diseased animal than the other, but the ratio of the two alleles was not completely consistent across all individuals, suggesting that there has been recombination or copy number variation in some subgroups of the cancer lineage.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data and represents an inference about recombination or copy number variation.

claims.claim: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were identified in several normal M. trossulus by qPCR.
claims.source: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were also identified in several normal M. trossulus. This confirms that H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claims.claim: H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population.
claims.source: The H4 cancer-associated alleles were also identified in several normal M. trossulus. This confirms that H4 alleles found in Mytilus BTN2 are present in some individuals in the normal M. trossulus population. This is expected, as each of the two transmissible cancer lineages arose in the past from a different normal M. trossulus individual.
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data and represents an expected finding given the origin of the cancer.

claims.claim: The C mitochondrial control region allele is present in M. chilensis cancers at a very low level (<1% of total allele fraction).
claims.source: Analysis of the two cancer-associated mitochondrial control region alleles shows that the C allele (only cloned from M. chilensis samples) is present in M. chilensis cancers at a very low level (<1% of total allele fraction).
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data from the study.

claims.claim: The C mitochondrial control region allele was undetectable in four of eight diseased M. edulis, suggesting that this heteroplasmy may be lost in some of the cancer cells spreading in the M. edulis population.
claims.source: It was also undetectable in four of eight diseased M. edulis, again suggesting that this heteroplasmy may be lost in some of the cancer cells spreading in the M. edulis population (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5 and represents an inference about heteroplasmy loss.

claims.claim: The D mitochondrial control region allele contains a tandem repeat with multiple copies of the control region.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, when comparing the copy number of the D allele to amplification at a conserved locus about 200 bp away (shown schematically in Figure 3B), the neoplastic samples yielded values greater than 100%. Further investigation revealed a tandem repeat in the D mitochondrial genome, with multiple copies of the control region that are targeted by allele-specific primers. results.result: Disseminated neoplasia in M. chilensis from Argentina and Chile is caused by a transmissible cancer lineage (Mytilus BTN2) that is distinct from the previously identified Mytilus BTN1. This conclusion is based on sequencing of the EF1α locus showing shared cancer-associated alleles (G and H) across diseased individuals from different geographic locations, and phylogenetic analysis demonstrating that these alleles are distinct from Mytilus BTN1.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 provide converging evidence from multiple diseased M. chilensis individuals across Argentina and Chile. The presence of four distinct EF1α alleles in diseased animals (C30), with two alleles (G and H) shared between individuals (C31, C32), strongly supports transmissible cancer. Phylogenetic analysis (C34, C35, C37) demonstrates these alleles are distinct from Mytilus BTN1, supporting the identification of a new lineage (C38). The data are internally consistent and the inference is well-supported.

results.result: Disseminated neoplasia in M. edulis from Europe is caused by the same transmissible cancer lineage (Mytilus BTN2) found in M. chilensis. Sequencing of EF1α from diseased M. edulis revealed cancer-associated alleles that exactly match those from M. chilensis (alleles G and H/H'), demonstrating that a single cancer lineage has crossed into two different host species.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 demonstrate that diseased M. edulis have more than two EF1α alleles (C39), with cancer-associated alleles exactly matching those from M. chilensis (C41). The presence of H and H' alleles (C42, C43) is consistent with polyploidy and de novo mutation after genome duplication. The exact sequence match between geographically distant samples from different species provides strong evidence for a single transmissible cancer lineage.

results.result: Analysis of the nuclear H4 locus confirms that Mytilus BTN2 is a distinct transmissible cancer lineage that arose from M. trossulus independently from Mytilus BTN1. Diseased M. chilensis and M. edulis share cancer-associated H4 alleles that are distinct from Mytilus BTN1 and match alleles found in some normal M. trossulus individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 provide independent confirmation using a second nuclear locus. The presence of 2-5 H4 alleles in diseased samples (C44), with cancer-associated alleles grouping together across species (C46) and being distinct from Mytilus BTN1 (C47), supports the Mytilus BTN2 identification. The finding that some normal M. trossulus carry these alleles (C48) is consistent with the cancer arising from M. trossulus (C49). This provides strong corroborating evidence for the EF1α results.

results.result: Mitochondrial control region analysis reveals that Mytilus BTN2 contains M. trossulus-derived mitochondrial alleles (C and D) that are distinct from Mytilus BTN1. These alleles are recombinants between female and male mitochondrial sequences, and evidence of mitochondrial heteroplasmy was found in M. chilensis samples. Phylogenetic analysis supports that Mytilus BTN1 and BTN2 arose from different M. trossulus individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 provide mitochondrial evidence supporting the distinctness of Mytilus BTN2. The identification of M. trossulus-like recombinant mitochondrial alleles (C51, C52, C54) that are distinct from Mytilus BTN1 (C57) and match previously reported Baltic sequences (C53) is well-documented. The presence of two recombinant alleles in M. chilensis (C54, C55) suggests heteroplasmy. Phylogenetic analysis (C58) supports independent origins of BTN1 and BTN2. The data are consistent and well-supported.

results.result: Mitochondrial COI sequencing confirms that Mytilus BTN2 is distinct from Mytilus BTN1 and originated from M. trossulus. The mtCOI allele (B) from Mytilus BTN2 is nested within M. trossulus sequences and is distinct from the Mytilus BTN1 allele. Evidence of mitochondrial recombination was found in Chilean M. chilensis samples, where the original Mytilus BTN2 mtCOI allele was replaced with a recombinant sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 provide additional mitochondrial evidence. The mtCOI phylogeny (C60) shows clear species separation with both BTN lineages nested within M. trossulus, and the Mytilus BTN2 allele (B) is distinct from Mytilus BTN1 (C61). The closest match to a Baltic M. trossulus sequence (C62) supports M. trossulus origin (C63). The absence of allele B in Chilean samples (C64) with evidence of recombination (C65) demonstrates mitochondrial dynamics within the cancer lineage. The data are internally consistent.

results.result: Quantitative PCR assays targeting cancer-associated alleles at EF1α and H4 loci confirm the presence of Mytilus BTN2 in diseased M. chilensis and M. edulis samples across multiple geographic locations. The EF1α qPCR assay showed 100% sensitivity and specificity for Mytilus BTN2 detection, with the cancer-associated allele present in all diagnosed diseased samples and absent in all normal samples. Two diseased M. chilensis from Chile lacked Mytilus BTN2 markers, suggesting they have conventional cancer or a different transmissible lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 and C82 demonstrate robust validation of the transmissible cancer identification using qPCR. The EF1α assay detected cancer-associated alleles in all Mytilus BTN2-positive samples including those not detected by cloning (C66), with no false positives in normal samples (C67, C70). The assay was negative in Canadian M. trossulus samples (C71), confirming distinctness from Mytilus BTN1. The identification of two Chilean samples without Mytilus BTN2 markers (C68, C69) demonstrates appropriate specificity. The claim of highest sensitivity and specificity for EF1α (C82) is supported by the data.

results.result: qPCR analysis of mitochondrial loci reveals complex mitochondrial dynamics in Mytilus BTN2, including heteroplasmy, tandem repeats, and mitochondrial replacement. The mtCR D allele contains a tandem repeat with multiple copies of the control region. The C allele is present at low levels in M. chilensis and is lost in some M. edulis samples. Chilean M. chilensis samples show complete replacement of the original mtCOI allele with a recombinant sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 document mitochondrial complexity in Mytilus BTN2. The variable ratio of H4 alleles (C73) suggests recombination or copy number variation. The presence of H4 alleles in normal M. trossulus (C74, C75) is expected given the cancer's origin. The low-level C allele (C76) and its loss in some M. edulis (C77) demonstrate heteroplasmy dynamics. The tandem repeat in the D allele (C78) is well-documented with sequencing confirmation. The mtCOI replacement in Chilean samples (C79, C80) is supported by qPCR data. These findings are internally consistent and well-supported.

results.result: SNP analysis using 13 diagnostic loci confirms that Mytilus BTN2 is derived from M. trossulus. All Mytilus BTN2-positive M. edulis and M. chilensis samples showed strong fluorescence for M. trossulus alleles at all diagnostic loci, while no normal animals showed M. trossulus signals at more than one locus. This provides independent multi-locus confirmation of the M. trossulus origin of Mytilus BTN2.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C83-C85 provide strong independent validation using SNP analysis. The consistent detection of M. trossulus alleles across all 13 diagnostic loci in cancer samples (C83) with clear separation from normal samples (C84) provides robust evidence. The multi-locus approach reduces the likelihood of false positives from introgression or hybridization. The conclusion that this supports M. trossulus origin (C85) is well-justified. The identification of two Chilean samples without Mytilus BTN2 (C81) is consistent with qPCR results.

results.result: Mytilus BTN2 is a single transmissible cancer lineage that originated in M. trossulus, is distinct from Mytilus BTN1, and has crossed into two new host species (M. chilensis and M. edulis) with global distribution across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Phylogenetic evidence from four loci and SNP data from 13 diagnostic loci demonstrate concordant gene trees consistent with a clonal, asexual cancer lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7, C87-C89, C126-C127 represent the major conclusions of the study. The M. trossulus origin (C3, C88) is supported by phylogenetic analysis of four loci and SNP data. The distinctness from Mytilus BTN1 (C4, C87) is demonstrated across all loci. The near-identity of cancers from M. chilensis and M. edulis (C5) and their global distribution (C6, C7, C127) are well-documented. The concordance of gene trees (C89) supports a clonal lineage. The evidence from multiple independent loci and methods provides strong support for these conclusions.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence rule out contamination as an explanation for the identical sequences found in M. chilensis and M. edulis samples. Initial sequencing was performed independently at different sites, qPCR was replicated in two labs, slight differences exist between subgroups, and qPCR confirms significant fractions of cancer-associated alleles in diseased samples but not normal samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 address a critical alternative explanation. The independent sequencing at different sites (C101), replication in two labs (C102), presence of slight differences between subgroups (C103), and qPCR confirmation of high allele fractions in diseased samples only (C104) provide strong evidence against contamination. The conclusion that the data represent genuine identification (C105) is well-justified. These controls are appropriate and strengthen confidence in the main findings.

results.result: Mytilus BTN2 exhibits dynamic mitochondrial evolution, including heteroplasmy, recombination with host mitochondria, and potential mitochondrial replacement. This mitochondrial dynamics may be a common feature among transmissible cancers, as similar mitochondrial capture has been observed in canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT).
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C116-C118 describe mitochondrial dynamics in Mytilus BTN2. The observation of mitochondrial recombination in Chilean samples (C90) is well-documented. The inference that this suggests dynamic mitochondrial populations (C116) is reasonable given the data. The comparison to CTVT (C117) is supported by citations. The speculation that this may be a common feature (C118) is appropriately cautious. The evidence supports the observations, though the generalization to other transmissible cancers is speculative.

results.result: The global distribution of Mytilus BTN2 across hemispheres and oceans is most likely due to anthropogenic transport via shipping vessels rather than natural ocean currents. Examples of accidental introduction of Mytilus species via shipping are well-documented, and this mechanism could facilitate worldwide spread of transmissible cancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 and C128 propose anthropogenic transport as the mechanism for global spread. While the observation of trans-hemispheric distribution is well-supported (C94), and ocean currents are unlikely to explain it (C95), the conclusion that shipping is the most likely mechanism (C96) is speculative. The supporting evidence of documented Mytilus introductions via shipping (C97, C98) and the biological plausibility (C99) strengthen the hypothesis, but direct evidence is lacking. The authors acknowledge this cannot be experimentally proven. The speculation about worldwide reach (C100, C128) is appropriately cautious but remains uncertain.

results.result: The cross-species transmission of Mytilus BTN2 into M. chilensis and M. edulis may be facilitated by the ability of Mytilus species to hybridize, and the close relationship between M. chilensis and M. edulis may have lowered barriers to transmission. This finding challenges the hypothesis that transmissible cancers primarily occur in inbred populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115 address mechanisms of cross-species transmission. The ability of Mytilus species to hybridize (C109) is well-established and provides a plausible mechanism for reduced barriers. The close relationship between M. chilensis and M. edulis (C112) is supported by citations, though controversial. The speculation about sequential transmission (C113) is reasonable but uncertain. The observation that Mytilus BTN2 spreads in outbred populations (C115) directly challenges prior hypotheses (C114) and is well-supported by the data. The main conclusion about challenging the inbreeding hypothesis is supported.

results.result: The age and geographic origin of Mytilus BTN2 remain uncertain. BLAST searches suggest closest matches to M. trossulus from the Baltic and British Columbia, and mitochondrial sequences match rare Baltic haplotypes more commonly found in Norway, suggesting a Northern European origin. However, the exact population of origin cannot be determined from available data.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 and C121-C125 address the age and origin of Mytilus BTN2. The age is explicitly stated as unknown (C91), with speculation about 50+ years if early reports are attributable to this lineage (C93). The BLAST results (C122) and mitochondrial sequence matches (C123) provide some evidence for Northern European origin (C124), but the authors appropriately conclude this remains uncertain (C125). The speculation about using sequence comparisons to identify origin (C121) is reasonable but not yet realized. The uncertainty is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Background information on transmissible cancers and disseminated neoplasia in bivalves and Mytilus species, including prior reports of the disease, geographic distribution, prevalence, and the previously identified Mytilus BTN1 lineage in Canadian M. trossulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C28 provide background context from prior literature. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to published work and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide necessary context for understanding the significance of the current findings. The information is accurately presented and well-supported by citations.

results.result: Invertebrates lack vertebrate-like adaptive immunity, and most prior BTN cases have been species-specific. Alternative explanations for the mitochondrial data include nuclear-to-mitochondrial transfer (numt), and mitochondrial replacement has not been previously described in BTN.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108, C119-C120 provide additional context and discuss alternative explanations. The lack of adaptive immunity in invertebrates (C106) is established knowledge. The species-specificity of most BTN cases (C107, C108) is supported by citations. The numt alternative explanation (C119) is appropriately raised as a possibility that cannot be excluded. The statement that mitochondrial replacement hasn't been described in BTN (C120) is a factual statement about current knowledge. These claims are well-supported.

results.result: The finding of a single cancer lineage crossing into multiple species across vast distances is characterized as unexpected.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is a statement of interpretation about the unexpectedness of the findings. Given that prior BTN cases were mostly species-specific (C107) and geographically limited, this characterization is reasonable and supported by the context of prior knowledge in the field.
